Summary of the Gaps: The good news is you are not starting from scratch. Strengths like Research Facilitation, Experiment Design, and Research Analysis carry straight over and give you a real head start. What is newer is the craft at the center of it, things like Heuristics, UX Research Method Selection, and Agile UX. You will also grow into the everyday work, like Analyzing Research Findings and Presenting Research Results. Just as important is how the work happens on a team. Practices like Shared Ownership, Empowerment, and Shared Leadership are less about tools and more about how you show up with the people around you. You will not learn all of this up front. Like the work itself, you grow into it a piece at a time, taking on a little more as you go.
Training Recommendations:
There is no single right path, but here is one sensible way to grow into it:
1. Start with Experiment Design, Vision Formation, and Customer Experience Strategy. These are the first skills to build, and getting them solid makes everything after it easier.
2. Get a feel for how teams actually run the work by learning a method like Google Design Sprint Method and Scrum Method.
3. Practice the real tasks on something small, like Analyzing Research Findings and Presenting Research Results, rather than only reading about them.
4. Pick up the common tools as you need them, like Figma, Notion, and Figjam, learning each one on a real task.
5. Build a couple of real examples you can show, like Competitive Analysis and User Journey Map, to prove the skills to yourself and others.
6. Grow the team habits this work runs on, like Shared Ownership and Empowerment, by using them with an actual team.

Through all of it, lean on what you already do well, like Research Facilitation and Experiment Design. Those strengths give you something to stand on while the newer skills catch up.

You will also grow into the everyday work, like Requirements Gathering and Requirements Refinement. Just as important is how the work happens on a team. Practices like Shared Ownership, Empowerment, and Shared Leadership are less about tools and more about how you show up with the people around you. You will not learn all of this up front. Like the work itself, you grow into it a piece at a time, taking on a little more as you go.
Training Recommendations:
There is no single right path, but here is one sensible way to grow into it:
1. Start with Requirements Management. These are the first skills to build, and getting them solid makes everything after it easier.
2. Get a feel for how teams actually run the work by learning a method like Scrum Method and Kanban Method.
3. Practice the real tasks on something small, like Requirements Gathering and Requirements Refinement, rather than only reading about them.
4. Pick up the common tools as you need them, like Notion, Figjam, and Trello, learning each one on a real task.
5. Build a couple of real examples you can show, like Problem Statements and Problem Checklists, to prove the skills to yourself and others.
6. Grow the team habits this work runs on, like Shared Ownership and Empowerment, by using them with an actual team.

Through all of it, lean on what you already do well, like Data Analysis and Problem-Solving. Those strengths give you something to stand on while the newer skills catch up.

2. Get a feel for how teams actually run the work by learning a method like Scrum Method and Kanban Method.
3. Practice the real tasks on something small, like Sprint Planning and Level of Effort Estimation, rather than only reading about them.
4. Pick up the common tools as you need them, like Notion, Figjam, and Zoom, learning each one on a real task.
5. Build a couple of real examples you can show, like Personal Growth Roadmap and Working Agreements, to prove the skills to yourself and others.
6. Grow the team habits this work runs on, like Shared Ownership and Empowerment, by using them with an actual team.

Through all of it, lean on what you already do well, like Building Influence and Buy-in Generation. Those strengths give you something to stand on while the newer skills catch up.

Summary of the Gaps: The good news is you are not starting from scratch. Strengths like Problem-Solving, Public Speaking, and Attention to Detail carry straight over and give you a real head start. What is newer is the craft at the center of it, things like Kanban Board Management, Storytelling, and Agile Coaching. You will also grow into the everyday work, like Sprint Planning and Level of Effort Estimation. Just as important is how the work happens on a team. Practices like Shared Ownership, Empowerment, and Shared Leadership are less about tools and more about how you show up with the people around you. You will not learn all of this up front. Like the work itself, you grow into it a piece at a time, taking on a little more as you go.
